findings.why: The tested recall-relevant procedure had two parts: (a) the target date was derived from the participant's own summary of how far before deadlines they usually finished, and (b) the participant wrote a scenario, built on problems met before, that ends at that typical time. The authors state that the study had no scenario-only condition, that they cannot say which part produced the realism, and that they cannot rule out that asking for a more pessimistic hypothetical scenario did the work. Only 12.5% of that group mentioned past experience in the thought listing. The item credits the reduction to having linked past experience to the new task, and its title and W praktyce#1 present the shorter compare-with-the-past step as the active ingredient; Ograniczenia says nothing about the two parts being inseparable. A reader may believe that looking up and comparing past tasks is what lowered the optimism, which the study cannot show.

findings.why: The authors say that, on the basis of their studies, they do not yet have compelling evidence that individuals can use recollections of their own past performance to improve the accuracy of their time estimates. They also report that estimates built heavily on typical past completion times would have been far too pessimistic, that participants did not incorporate their past experience directly into their predictions, and that an improvement is expected only if the recollections are valid and the present task is comparable. The item tells the reader to check the previous duration and only then set the date, yet Ograniczenia carries none of these four points; a reader may treat a past duration as the number to adopt, which in this study would have overshot, and the letter B may read as stronger support for that step than the authors themselves give. Upstream line 3 is the same look-up action, so the caveat applies to the inherited claim too.

findings.why: Participants in Study 4 did not set deadlines: a 1-week or 2-week deadline was assigned, and they privately predicted the date and time at which they would finish. Actual completion time depended strongly on the assigned deadline (about 4.3 versus 9.1 days) and was not changed by the thought-focus manipulation. Setting a deadline in W praktyce#1, and declaring one in Ocena redakcyjna#1 (przed deklaracją terminu), widen the action from predicting one's own finishing time to choosing or announcing a deadline, which was not tested, and the item does not mention that assigned deadlines moved actual time. The editorial-example label covers the wording but not the missing limitation.

findings.text: B — pojedynczy eksperyment z udziałem 123 studentów.
findings.why: 123 is the whole sample, split into three thought-focus conditions crossed with two deadlines. The two groups behind 60,0% and 29,3% had n = 40 and n = 41 (editorial arithmetic: 24 of 40 and 12 of 41). The third group (recall only, 38.1%) is not given, and the reported test is one omnibus chi-square over three groups. The item gives one-decimal percentages next to only the total sample, so a reader cannot see how small the compared groups are. The participants were psychology undergraduates taking part for course credit; the item says only studentów. The percentages and the 30,7 point difference themselves hold against Table 4.
